newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Low-profile Austria heads for first Euro polls.
newsitem.headline: Low-profile Austria heads for first Euro polls.

text.p: Austria goes into its first European Parliament elections on Sunday with a reputation as one of the quiet countries of the EU, rarely getting involved in EU business unless it has a specific interest in an issue.

Diplomats say that since it became an EU member 22 months ago with Sweden and Finland, Austria has kept a low profile, making quiet common cause with northern states on environment issues and often following its neighbour Germany.

One exception to Austria's role is its European commissioner, Franz Fischler. Widely respected for his handling of EU farm issues, Fischler has swiftly become a major influence in the EU executive, officals say.
A partially tongue-in-cheek "report card" on commissioners written by the London-based Economist magazine last month gave Fischler top marks.
But in governmental dealings, Austria is subdued.
"Typically, they are very quiet," said one EU diplomat. "It is only when they really have problems when they come out and say something."
It is a sharp contrast with fellow newcomer Sweden, which is known for being opinionated on many issues and for coming up with initiatives ranging from security policy to employment.
Austrian officials agree that their country has not sought the limelight in the 15-nation bloc.
"We don't bang on the table. That would be very un-Austrian," one senior government official said.
The Austrians say they have worked quietly on areas they really care about, in particular the environment. For example, Vienna campaigned against funding for eastern European nuclear power stations.
Austria has joined Italy in pushing for a sweeping civil rights clause to be included in the EU treaty -- providing EU protection for women, racial minorities, gays and the disabled.
It has also pressed for language to protect workers and encourage job creation to be incorporated formally into the EU treaty.
"We are showing the EU that a medium-sized country can make a good contribution," the Austrian government official said.
Vienna, however, does suffers in Brussels from a perception that it is in the shadow of Germany.
"They are quite often close to the German position, which is maybe not always so good for them," an EU diplomat said.
A perhaps apocryphal story heard in Brussels highlights the perception.

Asked to give his opinion on an issue, a senior Austrian official said Vienna agreed with Germany. Informed that Germany had not yet stated its opinion the official said: "Well, we will agree with it anyway."
